facts: I began using AI assistance for programming around the beginning of 2024, approximately two years before the original interview.
I accepted the one-to-two-year range for first AI programming use.
At work I use GitHub Copilot and Claude through its command-line interface, rather than knowing much about its browser or app versions.
I sometimes use ChatGPT on my phone while commuting for questions I am curious about; in the office I have Copilot.
I use ChatGPT for personal knowledge during my commute and also use other AI models not listed in the interview.
I think the additional AI models I use are covered by GitHub Copilot; I did not specify individual model names here.
AI is integrated into my IDE, which I find convenient.
As a lead developer I do not ask AI to design entire systems for me, because I do not consider it mature enough for that.
AI may not understand my work, the full system or how the bank operates as I do, so I plan designs myself and divide them into smaller pieces.
For design I ask AI smaller technical feasibility questions; I find this quicker than searching the internet myself.

AI is faster than Google for my technical design questions. I recall that around late 2023, when I first started experimenting, AI was not very good at coding; this timing is approximate and differs slightly from my earlier beginning-of-2024 estimate.
When I initially adopted AI, I mainly asked it to document what my code did or explain code fragments.
In the six months before the original interview I felt AI had become more mature and could plan tasks and execute smaller parts.
AI can execute smaller parts of a plan but often still makes mistakes. For coding I use it as assistance rather than searching Google.
My three main uses of AI are design assistance, coding assistance and documentation.
I rate AI use for writing code often, after considering very often, and debugging sometimes because I do not find it particularly good at debugging.
I use AI often for understanding unfamiliar code, though not every day, and often for refactoring because I find it good at that.
I use AI often to write tests and very often for documentation and explaining concepts or learning.
I confirmed my very-often rating for AI-assisted explaining concepts and learning.
My latest task, the day before the original interview, involved a service mostly coded by a colleague.
I oversaw that service from a design perspective; the colleague was on Easter vacation and it was failing to deploy to one environment, so I investigated.
Although Copilot is available, in the preceding couple of weeks I had mainly been using a CLI that can run within Visual Studio.
For the deployment investigation I opened the CLI and asked Claude to prepare an instruction file covering the whole solution to establish code context.
I consider proper context about the code and its flow important for AI coding tools.
After creating the instruction file for the deployment failure, I asked Claude several explanatory questions. It explained some of the code, but I also needed my own instincts.

For the recent deployment failure I relied on previous knowledge and asked Claude for two or three solutions before reaching a conclusion. AI was not particularly successful that day, although I generally find it much better than before.
Two days before the original interview I asked Claude to analyze code and explain what was happening, instead of reading the entire code myself; it gave me an explanation in about five steps.
The five-step Claude explanation helped me understand and investigate the code, saving time.
I usually ask Claude to review my changes before peer review so I can fix issues beforehand and save time.
For the deployment task I modified C# class files and release YAML files used to deploy images.
The release YAML files deploy my service to cloud containers on Kubernetes. I compared releases for a service that deployed correctly and one that did not.
I asked AI to compare the release YAML files for the working and nonworking services.
I did not provide a specific overall duration for the recent task; I said AI sometimes helps within minutes, but sometimes goes wrong and repeatedly waits for confirmation.
When AI gives useless results I abandon it and work manually. My experience varies daily, but it usually helps with smaller tasks.
I described the coding task I was looking at as a new requirement from the business.
In my general working day I write code very often, every day.
In my general work I review code very often.
In general work I fix bugs and debug very often, and do testing often.
I rated specification and working with requirements often, as confirmed by the interviewer; the transcript renders my response as 'Open'.
I rated writing documentation often rather than daily, because I do not prepare documentation every day.
I rated continuous learning very often in my general work.
Of my frequent development activities, coding takes the most time overall.
My most recent day involved troubleshooting; for a coding example I began recalling a separate framework task.
I work on a framework team whose framework other developers use to develop their APIs. A recent coding example involved multiple framework tasks.
My recent coding work concerned several tasks in the shared API framework; the transcript repeats my preceding description.
The recent framework work aimed to support multiple platforms, including Windows services and IIS.
To support multiple platforms in our framework, I implemented several tasks, including connecting to different cloud resources while running on Windows.
Analysis takes the longest in coding tasks; implementing code is easier once the analysis is done, and I can ask AI to handle some portions.
I use Copilot to implement some portions of coding tasks after analysis.
For the recent framework multi-platform task I used Claude Sonnet through Copilot and Claude CLI to code some parts and write tests.
I confirmed the recent framework multi-platform task was completed.
One way we verified the framework task was by writing integration test cases and checking that all passed.
For verification I may ask AI whether test cases are complete; internal bank tools measure code coverage and satisfied conditions, providing a theoretical quality indicator.
In addition to coverage and missing-case analysis, we verify by running the actual service or component in its environment.
We ran the framework implementation in production to confirm that it behaved as expected.
I sometimes work with unfamiliar code because my team has many systems and I maintain a high-level overview of most components.
It is difficult to know every concrete code detail of our systems, so I sometimes inspect code written by teammates; other teammates do the same.
I said this need to inspect teammates' code also applies within my team.
A recent unfamiliar-code example was the service written by a teammate who went on Easter vacation, which I then had to inspect.
For that unfamiliar service some business-reported issues involved an unsuccessful response. I asked Claude why the service returned that response and investigated possible causes.
Claude helped me walk through the unfamiliar service's details; I already had a high-level understanding but needed detailed code comprehension.

When changing code I did not write, I usually run existing test cases; I did not attribute this verification step mainly to AI. The transcript says the tests 'should fail', without specifying the intended sequence further.
My team and I treat Copilot as a peer programmer that can suggest and implement some code while I program other parts.
I review AI-written code and AI can review mine, but final verification remains my responsibility.
Another recent AI-assisted task involved bank-wide security concerns and an incident or bug reported by another team, prompting me to analyze how security was implemented.
Business services use our team's framework, so our team is responsible for providing security. There were no clear guidelines describing the extent of security implementation.
I needed to clarify which security measures existed and guidelines for developers using them. AI made this analysis easier.
Without AI I estimate reviewing the security-related classes and listing all cases would have taken me two or three days; instead I asked Claude to prepare a document.
Claude produced a detailed security document that I later shortened. I estimate the task took perhaps more than half a day with AI.
I find AI particularly good at analyzing what code does and producing documentation that I can subsequently review.
While reviewing the AI-generated security documentation, I noticed one missing case and wrote code to address it.
AI-assisted documentation helped me find a missing security case, which I fixed as a bug.
Claude inspected the code and generated the security document. I read the document and noticed that most cases were satisfied but one was not.
After recognizing an unsatisfied security case in the document, I considered it a gap and went into the code to fix it.
For the security analysis task I think AI changed my approach; I might not have found the bug myself.
I qualified my claim that I might not have independently found the security bug as uncertain.
I have completed many similar tasks without AI. Sometimes AI waits repeatedly for around fifteen minutes without finishing even while I get coffee, using excessive resources.
I am concerned that prolonged AI attempts consume many tokens and that AI services charge by token usage; I sometimes get tired of this behavior.
When AI struggles, I abandon it and code manually, including fixing bugs without AI. I acknowledge that I may not explain context well enough to AI, making even simple tasks difficult.
I find that AI can make even simple tasks difficult when it lacks the right context.
I do not blindly rely on AI-generated answers. I personally verify whether code produces the expected output for a given input.
For independent validation I sometimes clear Copilot's context, give it the code again without telling it that it generated it, and ask it to identify problems.
I regard reviewing generated code in a fresh AI context as one way to verify it.
I thought the interviewer covered most relevant topics, but I still believe AI needs to become more mature.
I believe AI genuinely increases the productivity of its users, but at the original interview I did not think it was ready to replace existing work as some vendors suggested when selling products.
